content: 1. Edible shellfish refers to molluscan shellfish that have had one or both of their shells removed. 2. Single-service articles are items such as tableware, carry-out utensils, and other disposable items like bags, containers, placemats, stirrers, straws, toothpicks, and wrappers, which are designed for one-time use by a single person. 3. Single-use articles include utensils and bulk food containers that are intended to be used once and then discarded. Examples include wax paper, butcher paper, plastic wrap, formed aluminum food containers, jars, plastic tubs or buckets, bread wrappers, pickle barrels, ketchup bottles, and large cans that do not meet specific material, durability, strength, and cleanability standards. 4. Slacking is the process of gradually increasing the temperature of a food item, such as allowing it to rise from -23°C (-10°F) to -4°C (25°F), to prepare it for deep-fat frying or to ensure even heat penetration during the cooking of previously block-frozen foods like spinach. 5. A smooth food-contact surface is one that is free of pits and inclusions, with a cleanability standard equal to or exceeding that of 100-grit stainless steel. Non-food-contact surfaces of equipment should have a finish comparable to commercial-grade hot-rolled steel, free of visible scale. Decks, bulkheads, or deckheads should have even, level surfaces without roughness or projections that would make cleaning difficult. 6. A spa pool is a pool supplied with potable or saltwater, with characteristics similar to a whirlpool spa. These include water temperatures between 30°C and 40°C (86°F to 104°F), bubbling or jetted water effects that break at or above the water surface, a depth of more than 1 meter (3 feet), and a tub volume exceeding 6 tons of water. 7. A spill-resistant vacuum breaker (SVB) is a modification to a pressure vacuum breaker (PVB) designed to minimize water spillage. 8. A spray pad is a play and water contact area specifically designed to prevent standing water. 9. A suction fitting in a recreational water facility is a fitting through which water is drawn directly by a pump. 10. A swimming pool is a recreational water facility with a depth greater than 1 meter. This definition excludes spa pools that meet this depth criterion. 11. Mounted equipment refers to non-portable equipment that is designed to be affixed off the floor, typically on a counter or shelf. 12. Tableware includes eating, drinking, and serving utensils such as flatware (forks, knives, spoons), hollowware (bowls, cups, serving dishes, tumblers), and plates. 13. Technical water is water that has not been chlorinated or pH-controlled onboard a vessel. It originates from bunkering, condensate collection, or seawater processed through evaporators or reverse osmosis systems and is intended for storage and use in the technical water system. 14. A temperature-measuring device (TMD) is any instrument, such as a thermometer, thermocouple, or thermistor, that measures the temperature of food, air, or water and provides a numerical reading in Celsius and/or Fahrenheit. 15. Time/temperature control for safety food (TCS) refers to food that requires specific time and temperature controls to prevent the growth of harmful microorganisms. This is also known as potentially hazardous food (PHF). 16. Transmission of infection refers to any mechanism by which an infectious agent spreads from a source or reservoir to another person. This can occur through direct transmission (immediate transfer of infectious agents to a receptive portal of entry) or indirect transmission (via an intermediate item, organism, or process, such as fomites or vectorborne modes). 17. Turnover in a recreational water facility refers to the circulation of a volume of water equal to the pool's total volume through the recirculation system. For baby-only water facilities, the entire water volume must pass through all parts of the system, including filtration, secondary ultraviolet (UV) disinfection, and halogenation, every 30 minutes. 18. A utensil is any food-contact implement or container used for storing, preparing, transporting, dispensing, selling, or serving food. Examples include kitchenware, tableware (multiuse, single-service, or single-use), gloves used in food handling, food temperature-measuring devices, and probe-type price or identification tags in contact with food. 19. A utility sink is any sink located in a food service area that is not intended for handwashing or warewashing. 20. A variance is a written document issued by the Vessel Sanitation Program (VSP) that authorizes a modification or waiver of one or more requirements of the guidelines, provided that, in the opinion of the VSP, no health hazard or nuisance will result from the modification or waiver. 21. A wading pool is a recreational water facility with a maximum depth of less than 1 meter. 22. Warewashing refers to the cleaning and sanitizing of tableware, utensils, and food-contact surfaces of equipment.
